subject: Mathematics
title: Rohan's Tile Shop: Squares and Cubes
hook: How does a tile shop owner calculate orders using perfect squares and cubes?

slides.title: A Square and A Cube
slides.storyContext: Rohan's tile shop needs to order ceramic tiles. His supplier charges by square meter for floor tiles and by cubic meter for storage boxes. Priya watches as Kumar Uncle teaches the math behind the order.

image.alt: A Square and A Cube — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: The Order Problem
slides.storyContext: A customer wants a 6 meter × 6 meter bathroom floor covered with 1 meter × 1 meter tiles. Rohan calculates: 6 × 6 = 36 tiles. But the supplier lists the area as "6 squared." Priya asks: what does that mean?

image.alt: The Order Problem — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Squares: Numbers That Multiply Themselves

points.label: Definition
points.text: When a number multiplies by itself, the result is a perfect square. If n × n = n², then n² is a perfect square.

example.problem: Rohan's customer has a square courtyard with side 7 meters. How many square meter tiles does he need?
example.solution: Area = 7 × 7 = 7² = 49 square meters. He needs 49 tiles.

slides.inSimpleWords: A perfect square is the result when you multiply a number by itself. 5 × 5 = 25, so 25 is a perfect square.

image.alt: Perfect Squares: Numbers That Multiply Themselves — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Finding Square Roots: Reversing Multiplication

points.label: Definition
points.text: The square root of a number n (written √n) is the number you multiply by itself to get n. If m² = n, then √n = m.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: If Rohan knows he needs exactly 81 tiles to cover a square floor, he can find the side: √81 = 9 meters.

example.problem: A square kitchen has area 144 square meters. What is the side length?
example.solution: Side length = √144 = 12 meters (because 12 × 12 = 144).

slides.inSimpleWords: The square root reverses squaring. If 9² = 81, then √81 = 9.

image.alt: Finding Square Roots: Reversing Multiplication — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Perfect Cubes: Volume in Three Dimensions

points.label: Definition
points.text: When a number multiplies by itself THREE times, the result is a perfect cube. If n × n × n = n³, then n³ is a perfect cube.

points.label: Real-world use
points.text: Rohan stores tiles in cubic boxes. A box with side 3 meters holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic meters of tiles.

example.problem: A storage room is a perfect cube with side 5 meters. What is its volume?
example.solution: Volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 5³ = 125 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: A perfect cube is the result when you multiply a number by itself three times. 4 × 4 × 4 = 64, so 64 is a perfect cube.

image.alt: Perfect Cubes: Volume in Three Dimensions — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Common Perfect Squares and Cubes

example.problem: Is 144 a perfect square? Is 125 a perfect cube?

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorizing the first 10–15 perfect squares and cubes helps you solve problems faster without a calculator.

image.alt: Common Perfect Squares and Cubes — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Recognizing Non-Perfect Squares and Cubes

points.label: Not every number is perfect
points.text: Numbers like 50, 100 (perfect), 127 (not perfect), etc. Some are perfect, many are not.

points.label: How to check
points.text: Try multiplying candidates. For 50: 7 × 7 = 49, 8 × 8 = 64. Since 49 < 50 < 64, 50 is not a perfect square.

example.problem: Is 48 a perfect cube?
example.solution: Try: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. Since 27 < 48 < 64, 48 is not a perfect cube.

slides.inSimpleWords: If no whole number multiplied by itself (or itself three times) equals your target, then the target is not a perfect square (or cube).

image.alt: Recognizing Non-Perfect Squares and Cubes — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Rohan's Final Order
slides.storyContext: Rohan receives a big order: customer needs 10 square meters of floor tiles (10 different 1m×1m designs) and a storage box with side 4 meters for leftover stock.

example.problem: How many cubic meters does the storage box hold?
example.solution: Volume of box = 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares measure area (2D), cubes measure volume (3D). Rohan uses both for his business.

image.alt: Rohan's Final Order — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: Your Turn: The Garden Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's school is building a square vegetable garden with side 8 meters, and a cube-shaped rainwater tank with side 2 meters.

example.problem: Find the garden area and tank volume.
example.solution: Garden area = 8² = 64 square meters. Tank volume = 2³ = 8 cubic meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember: squares use ², cubes use ³.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Garden Problem — A Square and A Cube

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A perfect square is n × n = n². Examples: 25 = 5², 100 = 10².
A square root (√n) reverses squaring. √25 = 5.
A perfect cube is n × n × n = n³. Examples: 8 = 2³, 125 = 5³.
Squares measure area (floors, tiles). Cubes measure volume (boxes, tanks).

slides.inSimpleWords: Squares and cubes help us calculate areas and volumes in real life.

image.alt: What We Learned — A Square and A Cube

subject: Mathematics
title: Divya's Number Hunt: Rational and Irrational
hook: Are all numbers fractions? Divya discovers the mystery of numbers that cannot be written as fractions.

slides.title: A Story of Numbers
slides.storyContext: Divya and Anand visit Ms. Sharma's class for a special lesson on numbers. Ms. Sharma asks: "Can every number be written as a fraction?" The answer surprises them.

slides.title: The Fraction Question
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma draws numbers on the board: 1/2, 3, -5, 7/4. Then she asks, "Can you write 3 as a fraction?" Anand says, "Yes! 3 = 3/1." Ms. Sharma smiles and says, "Good. But what about √2? Can you write that as a fraction?" The class goes silent.

image.alt: The Fraction Question — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Rational Numbers: Fractions We Can Write

points.label: Definition
points.text: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

example.problem: Is 2.5 a rational number?
example.solution: Yes. 2.5 = 25/10 = 5/2. Since it can be written as a fraction of two integers, it is rational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rational numbers are any numbers you can write as a fraction: whole numbers, decimals that stop, and repeating decimals.

image.alt: Rational Numbers: Fractions We Can Write — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Repeating Decimals Are Rational

points.label: Repeating decimals
points.text: Decimals like 0.333... (1/3) and 0.1666... (1/6) repeat forever but are still rational because they equal a fraction.

points.label: How to identify
points.text: If a decimal repeats the same digit or pattern endlessly, it is rational. Example: 0.123123123... repeats "123."

example.problem: Is 0.333... rational?
example.solution: Yes. 0.333... = 1/3. It repeats but equals a fraction, so it is rational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any decimal that repeats, no matter how long the pattern, can be written as a fraction.

slides.title: Irrational Numbers: Beyond Fractions

points.label: Definition
points.text: An irrational number CANNOT be written as p/q. Its decimal never stops and never repeats.

points.label: Famous examples
points.text: √2 ≈ 1.41421356..., π ≈ 3.14159265..., e ≈ 2.71828... These decimals go on forever with no repeating pattern.

example.problem: Is √2 rational or irrational?
example.solution: Irrational. √2 ≈ 1.414213562... Its decimal never ends and never repeats. It cannot be written as a fraction p/q.

slides.inSimpleWords: Irrational numbers are decimals that go on forever without repeating. You cannot write them as fractions.

image.alt: Irrational Numbers: Beyond Fractions — A Story of Numbers

slides.title: Square Roots and Irrational Numbers

points.label: Perfect squares
points.text: √1 = 1, √4 = 2, √9 = 3, √16 = 4, √25 = 5. These are all rational (integers).

points.label: Non-perfect squares
points.text: √2, √3, √5, √6, √7, √8, √10 are all irrational. Their decimals never end.

example.problem: Which is rational and which is irrational: √25 or √26?
example.solution: √25 = 5 (rational). √26 ≈ 5.099... (irrational—decimal never ends).

slides.inSimpleWords: Square roots of perfect squares are rational. Square roots of non-perfect squares are irrational.

slides.title: Real Numbers: The Complete Number Line

points.label: Definition
points.text: The set of all rational and irrational numbers together is called the real numbers. Every point on the number line is a real number.

points.label: Order
points.text: Real numbers include: negative integers, zero, positive integers, fractions, and irrationals. They can be ordered from smallest to largest.

example.problem: Order these from smallest to largest: -2, 1/2, √2, 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: The real number line contains all numbers—fractions, whole numbers, and never-ending decimals. Together, they form the complete real numbers.

slides.title: Ms. Sharma's Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ms. Sharma asks Divya and Anand to classify 10 numbers. They work together to sort them into rational and irrational.

example.problem: Is π irrational?
example.solution: Yes. π ≈ 3.141592653... Its decimal never ends and never repeats. π cannot be written as p/q.

slides.inSimpleWords: π is irrational because its decimal never terminates or repeats.

slides.title: Your Turn: Classify the Numbers
slides.storyContext: Divya and Anand give you a list: 7, 0.5, √9, √10, 22/7, π. Sort them into rational and irrational.

example.problem: Which are rational and which are irrational?

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember: if it can be written as a fraction, it is rational. If it cannot, it is irrational.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Rational numbers can be written as fractions p/q. Examples: 1/2, 3, 2.5, 0.333...
Irrational numbers cannot be written as fractions. Their decimals never end and never repeat. Examples: √2, π, e.
Real numbers include all rational and irrational numbers.
Square roots of perfect squares are rational; square roots of non-perfect squares are irrational.

slides.inSimpleWords: Not all numbers are fractions. Some numbers, like √2 and π, are irrational and cannot be written as fractions.

image.alt: What We Learned — A Story of Numbers

subject: Mathematics
title: Vikram's Sweet Shop: Expanding Expressions
hook: When Vikram distributes sweets to groups, the numbers multiply in unexpected ways. Learn the algebra of expansion.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: school friend learning algebra from Vikram

slides.title: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply
slides.storyContext: Vikram's sweet shop receives bulk orders. He uses algebra to calculate: if each customer wants (a + b) sweets from c different vendors, how many total? His method: distribute, then multiply.

slides.title: The Festival Order
slides.storyContext: A school festival orders sweets. Vikram knows: each of the 3 booths gets 2 types of sweets (gulab jamun and laddu). So each booth wants (2 + 3) sweets... wait, he realizes it's (g + l) where g = gulab jamun, l = laddu. When 5 shopkeepers each order the same mix (g + l), the total is 5(g + l). But how many sweets is that?

image.alt: The Festival Order — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: The Distributive Property: Multiply First, Then Add

points.label: Rule
points.text: a(b + c) = ab + ac. When you multiply a number outside brackets by the terms inside, multiply the outside number by EACH term inside.

points.label: Why?
points.text: Imagine 3 bags, each with (2 apples + 4 oranges). Total apples = 3 × 2 = 6. Total oranges = 3 × 4 = 12. Total fruit = 6 + 12 = 18. So 3(2 + 4) = 6 + 12.

example.problem: Expand 5(g + l) where g = gulab jamun, l = laddu.
example.solution: 5(g + l) = 5g + 5l. If each sweet costs the same, Vikram counts: 5 gulab jamun and 5 laddu.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you see a number outside brackets, multiply that number by EVERY term inside the brackets.

slides.title: Expanding with Subtraction

points.label: Rule
points.text: a(b - c) = ab - ac. The distributive property works the same with subtraction.

points.label: Examples
points.text: 3(x - 2) = 3x - 6. If a shop sells (price - discount), and you buy 3, you pay 3price - 3discount.

example.problem: A customer buys 4 boxes. Each box has (x chocolates - 2 damaged). How many good chocolates total?
example.solution: 4(x - 2) = 4x - 8 good chocolates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction in brackets: multiply the outside number by each term, and keep the minus sign.

image.alt: Expanding with Subtraction — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: Expanding Two Brackets: (a + b)(c + d)

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Multiply EVERY term in the first bracket by EVERY term in the second.

points.label: Method (FOIL)
points.text: First: a × c. Outer: a × d. Inner: b × c. Last: b × d. Then add all four.

example.problem: Vikram arranges sweets in (x + 3) rows and (y + 2) columns. How many sweets total?

slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying two brackets, each term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. You get four products; add them all.

image.alt: Expanding Two Brackets: (a + b)(c + d) — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: Perfect Square Expansion: (a + b)² and (a - b)²

points.label: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
points.text: Example: (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9.

points.label: (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²
points.text: Example: (x - 2)² = x² - 4x + 4.

example.problem: A square sweet box has side (a + 5). What is its area?
example.solution: Area = (a + 5)² = a² + 10a + 25 square units.

slides.inSimpleWords: For (a + b)²: square the first term, double the product, then square the second term. (a - b)² is the same but the middle term is negative.

slides.title: Difference of Squares: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b²

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b². When the same terms add in one bracket and subtract in the other, the middle cancels.

points.label: Quick factoring
points.text: If you see a² - b², it factors as (a + b)(a - b). Useful for checking work and simplifying.

example.problem: Expand (x + 4)(x - 4).
example.solution: (x + 4)(x - 4) = x² - 16. Notice: no middle term! The +4x and -4x cancel.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two brackets have the same terms but opposite signs (one + one -), multiply to get: (first term)² - (second term)².

slides.title: Vikram's Real Order
slides.storyContext: A restaurant orders sweets in (2x + 3) boxes of (x + 2) sweets each. Vikram must calculate the total.

example.problem: Find the total number of sweets in (2x + 3)(x + 2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand by multiplying every term in the first bracket by every term in the second, then combine like terms.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Sweet Box Problem
slides.storyContext: Maya designs a box with dimensions (a + 5) by (a + 5) by (a + 3). What is the volume?

example.problem: Find the volume of a box with dimensions (a + 5) × (a + 5) × (a + 3).
example.solution: First, (a + 5)² = a² + 10a + 25. Then multiply by (a + 3): (a² + 10a + 25)(a + 3) = a³ + 3a² + 10a² + 30a + 25a + 75 = a³ + 13a² + 55a + 75.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand step by step: first expand the square, then multiply the result by the third dimension.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Sweet Box Problem — We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Distributive property: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Expanding two brackets: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.
Perfect squares: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b².
Difference of squares: (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b².

slides.inSimpleWords: Expanding means removing brackets by multiplying and adding terms. Master these patterns to simplify algebra.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Kitchen: Rational Expressions and Algebraic Fractions
hook: Arjun mixes recipes and splits bills. Learn how fractions hide inside algebra.

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise
slides.storyContext: Arjun's restaurant needs to scale recipes, split bills, and manage ingredient ratios. He discovers that algebra and fractions work together—algebraic fractions appear everywhere.

image.alt: Fractions in Disguise — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: The Recipe Scaling Problem
slides.storyContext: A recipe needs (x/2) liters of milk for (x + 1) people. Aman asks: "If the recipe is halved, how much milk per person?" Arjun realizes: the answer is a fraction of a fraction—an algebraic fraction: (x/2) ÷ (x + 1) = x / (2(x + 1)).

image.alt: The Recipe Scaling Problem — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Algebraic Fractions: Fractions with Variables

points.label: Definition
points.text: An algebraic fraction is a fraction where the numerator and/or denominator contain variables (letters). Examples: x/5, 3/(x + 1), (x + 2)/(2x - 1).

points.label: Key rule
points.text: The denominator can NEVER be zero. If x/(x - 3), then x ≠ 3 (because 3 - 3 = 0).

example.problem: In the fraction (2x + 3)/(x - 5), what value of x is NOT allowed?
example.solution: x ≠ 5, because when x = 5, the denominator becomes 5 - 5 = 0, and division by zero is undefined.

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebraic fractions are just fractions, but they use letters. Always remember: the denominator cannot be zero.

image.alt: Algebraic Fractions: Fractions with Variables — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Method
points.text: Factor the numerator and denominator. Cancel common factors. What remains is the simplified fraction.

example.problem: Simplify (4x + 8) / (2x + 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: To simplify: factor both the top and bottom, then cancel any common factors.

image.alt: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Multiplying Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac) / (bd). Multiply tops and multiply bottoms.

points.label: Simplify first
points.text: Before multiplying, cancel common factors across the fractions. This saves work.

example.problem: Multiply (3x / 4) × (2 / x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions by multiplying the tops together and the bottoms together. Then simplify.

image.alt: Multiplying Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Dividing Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). Flip the second fraction, then multiply.

slides.inSimpleWords: To divide fractions: flip the second fraction and multiply.

image.alt: Dividing Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Same denominator
points.text: (a/c) + (b/c) = (a + b) / c. Just add the numerators.

points.label: Different denominators
points.text: Find a common denominator, convert each fraction, then add. Example: 1/x + 1/2 = 2/(2x) + x/(2x) = (2 + x) / (2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: To add/subtract: get the same denominator, combine the numerators, then simplify.

image.alt: Adding and Subtracting Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Arjun's Real Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun's restaurant budget is split: (2x + 5) rupees for ingredients, (x - 1) rupees for labor. The total cost per meal is 1 / [(2x + 5) / (x - 1)] rupees. Simplify this.

example.problem: Simplify 1 / [(2x + 5) / (x - 1)].

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Bill Split
slides.storyContext: Three friends split a restaurant bill of (3x² + 6x) rupees equally among (x + 2) people. How much per person?

example.problem: Simplify (3x² + 6x) / (x + 2).
example.solution: Factor: 3x(x + 2) / (x + 2) = 3x (after canceling (x + 2)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor the numerator, cancel common terms with the denominator, and simplify.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Algebraic fractions have variables in numerator or denominator. The denominator can never be zero.
Simplify by factoring and canceling common factors.
Multiply: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac)/(bd). Divide: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
Add/subtract: find a common denominator first, then combine.

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebraic fractions work like regular fractions—use the same rules, but with variables.

image.alt: What We Learned — Fractions in Disguise

subject: Mathematics
title: Pradeep's Field: The Right Triangle Mystery
hook: An ancient Indian mathematician and a Greek one both discovered the same truth about right triangles. Pradeep finds it in his farm.

slides.title: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
slides.storyContext: Pradeep's square field must be divided by a diagonal fence into two right triangles. How long is the diagonal? Shastri tells him of an ancient formula discovered in India over 2000 years ago.

image.alt: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Measuring the Diagonal
slides.storyContext: Pradeep has a square plot 12 meters × 12 meters. He wants to fence diagonally. To calculate the fence length, Shastri says: "In ancient India, Baudhayana wrote: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides." Pradeep realizes this solves his problem.

image.alt: Measuring the Diagonal — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: The Theorem: a² + b² = c²

points.label: Statement
points.text: In a right triangle, if the two legs (shorter sides) are a and b, and the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle) is c, then: a² + b² = c².

points.label: Which side is which?
points.text: The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle (90° angle). The legs meet at the right angle.

example.problem: In a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, what is the hypotenuse?

slides.inSimpleWords: In any right triangle, if you square the two shorter sides and add them, you get the square of the longest side.

image.alt: The Theorem: a² + b² = c² — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Finding the Hypotenuse

points.label: Given legs a and b
points.text: Use c² = a² + b², then take the square root: c = √(a² + b²).

example.problem: A ladder leans against a wall. The base is 6 meters from the wall, the wall is 8 meters tall. How long is the ladder?
example.solution: This forms a right triangle with legs 6 and 8. Ladder = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the hypotenuse: square both legs, add them, then take the square root.

image.alt: Finding the Hypotenuse — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Finding a Missing Leg

points.label: If you know c and a, find b
points.text: Rearrange: b² = c² - a², so b = √(c² - a²).

points.label: Example
points.text: Hypotenuse 13, one leg 5: other leg = √(169 - 25) = √144 = 12.

example.problem: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15 and one leg 9. Find the other leg.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find a missing leg: square the hypotenuse, subtract the square of the other leg, then take the square root.

image.alt: Finding a Missing Leg — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Pythagorean Triples: Special Whole-Number Triangles

points.label: Definition
points.text: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers a, b, c where a² + b² = c². All three sides are integers—no square roots needed.

example.problem: Is (6, 8, 10) a Pythagorean triple?
example.solution: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². Yes, it is a Pythagorean triple (and it is 2 × (3, 4, 5)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Pythagorean triples are right triangles where all three sides are whole numbers. They are very useful for quick calculations.

image.alt: Pythagorean Triples: Special Whole-Number Triangles — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Proving a Right Triangle: Converse of the Theorem

points.label: Converse
points.text: If a² + b² = c² is true, then the triangle is a right triangle. You can use this to check if a triangle is right-angled.

points.label: Example
points.text: Sides 5, 12, 13: check 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². Yes, it is right-angled.

example.problem: Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?
example.solution: Check: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². Yes, it is right-angled.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two sides squared and added equal the third side squared, then that triangle has a right angle.

image.alt: Proving a Right Triangle: Converse of the Theorem — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Pradeep's Diagonal
slides.storyContext: Pradeep's square field is 12 meters × 12 meters. The diagonal creates two right triangles with legs 12 and 12.

example.problem: Find the diagonal length of a 12 × 12 meter square field.
example.solution: Diagonal² = 12² + 12² = 144 + 144 = 288. Diagonal = √288 = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: The diagonal of a square with side a is a√2.

image.alt: Pradeep's Diagonal — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Your Turn: The Village Path
slides.storyContext: A village path goes 9 meters east, then 12 meters north. What is the straight-line distance from start to end?

example.problem: Find the straight-line distance when traveling 9 meters east and 12 meters north.
example.solution: This forms a right triangle with legs 9 and 12. Distance = √(9² + 12²) = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two perpendicular paths form a right angle, the direct distance is found using the Pythagorean theorem.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Village Path — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: The Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c² for any right triangle.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
Find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²). Find a leg: a = √(c² - b²).
Pythagorean triples are whole-number right triangles like (3, 4, 5).
Check if a triangle is right-angled using the converse: if a² + b² = c², it is right-angled.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Pythagorean theorem connects the sides of any right triangle. Master the two steps: square, add (or subtract), then root.

image.alt: What We Learned — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Recipe and Ratios: Direct and Inverse Proportion
hook: Meera discovers that some quantities always stay in balance—when one doubles, so does the other. But some work the opposite way.

slides.title: Proportional Reasoning-2
slides.storyContext: Meera scales recipes for her bakery. When she doubles the flour, the cookies double. But when more workers arrive, the work gets done faster. Grandma explains: two different kinds of proportion.

image.alt: Proportional Reasoning-2 — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: The Cookie Mystery
slides.storyContext: Meera's cookie recipe needs 2 cups of flour for 24 cookies. Dev asks: "How much flour for 48 cookies?" Meera: "Double the flour, double the cookies—4 cups!" Then Grandma says: "But here's the twist: if 2 workers frost 24 cookies in 1 hour, how long for 1 worker?" Dev hesitates. Grandma smiles: "That is inverse proportion."

image.alt: The Cookie Mystery — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Direct Proportion: Both Increase Together

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are directly proportional if when one increases, the other increases by the same factor. If one doubles, so does the other. If one halves, so does the other.

points.label: Formula
points.text: If y is directly proportional to x, then y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.

example.problem: A recipe needs 3 eggs for 12 cookies. How many eggs for 36 cookies?
example.solution: Cookies tripled (12 → 36), so eggs triple: 3 → 9 eggs. Or using y = kx: k = 3/12 = 1/4, so for 36 cookies: eggs = (1/4) × 36 = 9.

slides.inSimpleWords: In direct proportion, when one thing grows, the other grows in the same way. Double one, double the other.

image.alt: Direct Proportion: Both Increase Together — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Finding the Constant of Proportionality

points.label: Method
points.text: If y = kx, then k = y/x. Divide corresponding values to find k.

points.label: Check consistency
points.text: Calculate k for multiple pairs. If k is always the same, the quantities are directly proportional.

example.problem: Does this data show direct proportion? (cost Rs 10 for 5 items, Rs 20 for 10 items, Rs 30 for 15 items)
example.solution: k = 10/5 = 2, k = 20/10 = 2, k = 30/15 = 2. Yes, k is constant at 2. The equation is cost = 2 × items.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check if quantities are directly proportional: divide one by the other for each pair. If the ratio is always the same, they are directly proportional.

image.alt: Finding the Constant of Proportionality — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Inverse Proportion: One Increases, the Other Decreases

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are inversely proportional if when one increases, the other decreases by the same factor. If one doubles, the other halves.

points.label: Formula
points.text: If y is inversely proportional to x, then y = k/x, or xy = k, where k is the constant of proportionality.

example.problem: 2 workers frost 24 cookies in 1 hour. How long would 1 worker take?
example.solution: Fewer workers → more time. Workers halved (2 → 1), so time doubles (1 → 2 hours). Using xy = k: 2 × 1 = 2, and 1 × 2 = 2. Both give k = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: In inverse proportion, when one thing doubles, the other halves. They multiply to a constant.

image.alt: Inverse Proportion: One Increases, the Other Decreases — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Speed, Time, and Distance: A Classic Inverse Case

points.label: Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time, or Time = Distance / Speed. If distance is fixed and speed doubles, time halves.

points.label: Example
points.text: To travel 120 km: at 40 km/h takes 3 hours; at 60 km/h takes 2 hours; at 80 km/h takes 1.5 hours.

example.problem: A 300 km trip takes 5 hours at one speed. How long at double the speed?
example.solution: Original: Time = 300/60 = 5 hours (speed = 60 km/h). Double speed: 120 km/h. New time = 300/120 = 2.5 hours (halved).

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed and time are inversely proportional for a fixed distance. Double the speed, half the time.

image.alt: Speed, Time, and Distance: A Classic Inverse Case — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Recognizing and Checking Inverse Proportion

points.label: Method
points.text: Multiply corresponding x and y values. If the product is always the same (constant k), the quantities are inversely proportional.

points.label: Example
points.text: Workers and time to finish: (2 workers, 3 hours), (3 workers, 2 hours), (6 workers, 1 hour). Check: 2×3=6, 3×2=6, 6×1=6. All equal, so inversely proportional.

example.problem: Is this inverse proportion? (pressure 2 atm, volume 60L), (3 atm, 40L), (4 atm, 30L)
example.solution: Check products: 2×60=120, 3×40=120, 4×30=120. All equal, so yes, inversely proportional. k = 120.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check inverse proportion: multiply corresponding values. If the product is always the same, they are inversely proportional.

image.alt: Recognizing and Checking Inverse Proportion — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Meera's Bakery Scaling
slides.storyContext: Meera receives orders for 1, 2, and 3 batches of cookies. Direct proportion: flour amounts scale. But workers and time scale inversely.

example.problem: Meera's recipe (1 batch): 2 cups flour, 4 workers frost 12 cookies/hour. For 3 batches, how much flour and how many hours for 1 worker to frost?
example.solution: Flour (direct): 2 × 3 = 6 cups. Frosting rate: 4 workers frost 12 cookies/hour means 1 worker frosts 3 cookies/hour. For 36 cookies (3 batches): time = 36/3 = 12 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ingredients scale directly with batch size. Time scales inversely with number of workers.

image.alt: Meera's Bakery Scaling — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Your Turn: The Water Tank Problem
slides.storyContext: A water tank fills at different rates. 2 pumps fill it in 6 hours. How long with 3 pumps?

example.problem: 2 pumps fill a tank in 6 hours. How long with 3 pumps?
example.solution: Pumps and time are inversely proportional. More pumps → faster filling. 2 × 6 = 12 (constant). With 3 pumps: 3 × time = 12, so time = 4 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: When more pumps work together, the job finishes faster. This is inverse proportion.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Water Tank Problem — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Direct proportion: y = kx. When one increases, so does the other by the same factor. Check by dividing: y/x = k (constant).
Inverse proportion: y = k/x or xy = k. When one increases, the other decreases. Check by multiplying: x × y = k (constant).
Recipes and ingredients: direct. Workers and time: inverse.
Speed and time (fixed distance): inverse. Distance and cost at fixed rate: direct.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two quantities either grow together (direct) or grow in opposite directions (inverse). Check by dividing (direct) or multiplying (inverse).

image.alt: What We Learned — Proportional Reasoning-2

subject: Mathematics
title: Isha's Architecture: Polygons, Shapes, and Symmetry
hook: Isha designs buildings and discovers that shapes have hidden patterns—sides, angles, and perfect reflections.

slides.title: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
slides.storyContext: Isha designs a new school building in Bangalore. Each room has different shapes—rectangles, pentagons, hexagons. Mr. Patel teaches her the properties of each and the hidden symmetries.

slides.title: The Design Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha sketches: square classrooms, triangular roofs, hexagonal lunch hall. Rohan asks: "Why hexagons?" Mr. Patel explains: "Hexagons are strong, efficient, and have beautiful symmetry. Let me teach you about polygons."

slides.title: Polygons: Sides, Vertices, and Angles

points.label: Definition
points.text: A polygon is a closed plane figure made of straight line segments. The sides don't cross. Vertices are the corners where sides meet.

points.label: Naming
points.text: Triangles (3 sides), quadrilaterals (4), pentagons (5), hexagons (6), heptagons (7), octagons (8), nonagons (9), decagons (10).

example.problem: How many vertices does a hexagon have?
example.solution: A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 vertices (one at each corner).

slides.inSimpleWords: A polygon is a closed shape made of straight sides. The number of sides = number of vertices.

slides.title: Sum of Interior Angles

points.label: Formula
points.text: For any polygon with n sides, the sum of interior angles = (n - 2) × 180°.

example.problem: What is the sum of interior angles in a pentagon?
example.solution: Pentagon has 5 sides. Sum = (5 - 2) × 180° = 3 × 180° = 540°.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the sum of all angles inside a polygon: count sides (n), subtract 2, multiply by 180°.

slides.title: Regular Polygons: All Sides and Angles Equal

points.label: Definition
points.text: A regular polygon has all sides of equal length and all angles of equal measure. Examples: equilateral triangle, square, regular hexagon.

points.label: Each angle in a regular polygon
points.text: Each interior angle = [(n - 2) × 180°] / n.

example.problem: What is each interior angle in a regular octagon?

slides.inSimpleWords: A regular polygon looks the same no matter how you rotate it. All sides are equal, all angles are equal.

slides.title: Line Symmetry: Mirror Images

points.label: Definition
points.text: A shape has line symmetry if it can be folded along a line so that both halves match perfectly. That line is called a line of symmetry.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square: 4 lines of symmetry. Rectangle: 2. Circle: infinite. Equilateral triangle: 3. Isosceles triangle: 1.

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
example.solution: A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry: 3 through opposite vertices and 3 through midpoints of opposite sides.

slides.inSimpleWords: Line symmetry means you can fold the shape along a line and both halves look identical.

slides.title: Rotational Symmetry: Spinning Into Place

points.label: Definition
points.text: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same when rotated less than 360° around a central point. The order of rotational symmetry is how many times it matches itself in one full rotation.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Square: order 4 (matches at 90°, 180°, 270°, 360°). Equilateral triangle: order 3. Regular hexagon: order 6.

example.problem: A shape matches itself when rotated 60°. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
example.solution: 360° / 60° = 6. The shape has rotational symmetry of order 6 (like a regular hexagon).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotational symmetry means the shape looks the same when you spin it around. The more it matches itself, the higher the order.

slides.title: Properties of Common Quadrilaterals

points.label: Square
points.text: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles (90°), diagonals equal and perpendicular. 4 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 4.

points.label: Rectangle
points.text: Opposite sides equal, 4 right angles, diagonals equal but not perpendicular. 2 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 2.

points.label: Rhombus
points.text: 4 equal sides, opposite angles equal, diagonals perpendicular. 2 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 2.

points.label: Parallelogram
points.text: Opposite sides equal and parallel, opposite angles equal. No line symmetry, but rotational symmetry of order 2.

example.problem: A shape is a rectangle. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
example.solution: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry (one through the midpoints of opposite long sides, one through midpoints of opposite short sides).

slides.inSimpleWords: Different quadrilaterals have different symmetries. Squares have the most; general parallelograms have the least.

image.alt: Properties of Common Quadrilaterals — Exploring Some Geometric Themes

slides.title: Isha's Hexagon Lunch Hall
slides.storyContext: Isha designs a regular hexagon-shaped lunch hall. Mr. Patel asks: find the sum of interior angles and the number of symmetries.

example.problem: A regular hexagon: find sum of interior angles and number of lines of symmetry.
example.solution: Sum = (6 - 2) × 180° = 720°. Each angle = 720° / 6 = 120°. Lines of symmetry = 6 (3 through vertices, 3 through edge midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular hexagons are strong and symmetric—perfect for buildings.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Tile Pattern
slides.storyContext: Isha tiles a floor with regular octagons and squares. How many lines of symmetry does a regular octagon have?

example.problem: Find the sum of interior angles in a regular octagon and its line symmetry.
example.solution: Sum = (8 - 2) × 180° = 1080°. Each angle = 135°. Lines of symmetry = 8 (4 through opposite vertices, 4 through edge midpoints).

slides.inSimpleWords: Regular octagons also tile well and have high symmetry.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Polygons are closed shapes with straight sides. A polygon with n sides has n vertices and sum of angles = (n-2)×180°.
Regular polygons have all sides equal and all angles equal. Each angle = [(n-2)×180°]/n.
Line symmetry: fold and both halves match. Rotational symmetry: rotate and the shape matches itself.
Quadrilaterals: square (most symmetric), rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram (least symmetric).

slides.inSimpleWords: Geometry is everywhere—in buildings, tiles, and nature. Symmetry and shapes reveal the hidden order.
